explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome) results from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery supplying the medial medulla. It classically produces a triad of deficits: contralateral hemiplegia due to corticospinal tract involvement in the pyramid, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch due to medial lemniscus damage, and ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy because the hypoglossal nucleus and nerve fascicles lie in the medial medulla.
keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome = contralateral hemiplegia + contralateral proprioception loss + ipsilateral CN XII palsy.

explanation: The anterior spinal artery descends in the midline of the medulla and supplies the medial zone, which includes the pyramid (corticospinal tract), medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus. The posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal medulla (gracile and cuneate nuclei), while the posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral medulla. The basilar artery supplies the pons, and the posterior cerebral artery supplies midbrain and occipital cortex.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies the pyramid and medial medulla.

explanation: The anterior spinal artery irrigates the medial two-thirds of the medulla, including the pyramidal upper motor neurons, hypoglossal nucleus and tongue muscles, and the medial lemniscus (which carries fine touch and proprioception after decussation). However, the second-order neurons of conscious proprioception—the gracile and cuneate nuclei—are located in the dorsal medulla and receive blood supply from posterior spinal artery branches, not the anterior spinal artery.
keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei (2nd order proprioceptive neurons) are dorsal and NOT supplied by the anterior spinal artery.

explanation: The ventral surface of the medulla displays key external landmarks including the anterior median fissure, pyramids, olives, and cranial nerve rootlets. Understanding this surface anatomy is essential for identifying the exit points of cranial nerves XII, IX, X, and XI, as well as locating the pyramidal decussation clinically.
keyConcept: Ventral medulla: pyramid, olive, preolivary/postolivary sulci with CN XII, IX, X, XI rootlets.
modelAnswer: The ventral surface of the medulla oblongata is marked by a deep anterior median fissure. On either side lie the medullary pyramids containing corticospinal fibers, which decussate at the caudal end as the pyramidal decussation. Lateral to each pyramid lies the preolivary sulcus, from which hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) rootlets emerge. Lateral to the olive (overlying the inferior olivary nucleus) lies the postolivary sulcus, from which glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and accessory (CN XI) nerve rootlets emerge in superior to inferior order.

explanation: The ventral surface of the pons features the basilar sulcus, pontomedullary junction, and attachment points for cranial nerves V, VI, VII, and VIII. Recognizing the relative positions of these nerves is clinically important for localizing pontine and cerebellopontine angle lesions.
keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar sulcus; CN V (lateral), CN VI/VII/VIII at pontomedullary junction.
modelAnswer: The ventral surface of the pons is convex and marked by a shallow median basilar sulcus housing the basilar artery. It is bounded superiorly by the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain and inferiorly by the medulla. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) emerges from the lateral aspect of the pons. At the lower border of the pons, between pons and medulla, emerge the abducens nerve (CN VI, most medial), facial nerve (CN VII), nervus intermedius, and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII, most lateral).

explanation: The ventral midbrain consists of paired cerebral peduncles separated by the interpeduncular fossa. The oculomotor nerve emerges from the medial side of each peduncle. This region contains critical descending motor pathways and is a key landmark for midbrain anatomy.
keyConcept: Ventral midbrain: cerebral peduncles, interpeduncular fossa, CN III emerges medially.
modelAnswer: The ventral surface of the midbrain is formed by two massive cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) separated by the interpeduncular fossa. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the medial side of each crus near the interpeduncular fossa. Deep to the crus lies the substantia nigra. The peduncles contain descending corticospinal, corticonuclear, and corticopontine fiber tracts. The optic tracts wind around the lateral aspects of the peduncles.

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a diamond-shaped depression on the ventral midbrain. Its boundaries include the optic chiasma, optic tracts, cerebral peduncles, and pons. Its contents are important hypothalamic and midbrain structures.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa: diamond-shaped depression bounded by optic chiasma, optic tracts, peduncles, and pons.
modelAnswer: The interpeduncular fossa is a diamond-shaped depression on the inferior surface of the midbrain. Its boundaries are: anteriorly the optic chiasma, anterolaterally the optic tracts, laterally the cerebral peduncles, and posteriorly the upper border of the pons. Its contents include the tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and the emerging oculomotor nerves (CN III).

explanation: The dorsal medulla has a closed part (with gracile and cuneate tubercles) and an open part that forms the floor of the fourth ventricle. Key surface landmarks identify underlying nuclei and are clinically relevant for localizing dorsal medullary lesions.
keyConcept: Dorsal medulla: gracile/cuneate tubercles (closed part); hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones (open part).
modelAnswer: The dorsal surface of the medulla has a lower closed part and an upper open part. The closed part displays the gracile tubercle medially (overlying the gracile nucleus) and cuneate tubercle laterally (overlying the cuneate nucleus), separated by the dorsal intermediate sulcus. The open part forms the lower half of the floor of the fourth ventricle, showing the hypoglossal trigone (medial), vagal trigone, vestibular trigone (between limbs of inferior fovea), area postrema, and striae medullares at the pontomedullary junction.

explanation: The dorsal pons forms the upper half of the floor of the fourth ventricle. It contains important landmarks such as the facial colliculus, locus coeruleus, and vestibular area, which correspond to underlying cranial nerve nuclei and tracts.
keyConcept: Dorsal pons forms upper half of 4th ventricle floor; contains facial colliculus and locus coeruleus.
modelAnswer: The dorsal surface of the pons forms the upper half of the floor of the fourth ventricle (rhomboid fossa). It features the median sulcus, medial eminence, facial colliculus, superior fovea, sulcus limitans, vestibular area, acoustic tubercle, and locus coeruleus. The superior cerebellar peduncles form the lateral boundaries of the upper part of the ventricle, and the striae medullares run transversely from lateral to medial across the pontomedullary junction.

explanation: The dorsal midbrain (quadrigeminal plate or tectum) consists of the superior and inferior colliculi, which are involved in visual and auditory reflexes respectively. The trochlear nerve emerges uniquely from the dorsal midbrain.
keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain = quadrigeminal plate with superior colliculi (visual) and inferior colliculi (auditory).
modelAnswer: The dorsal surface of the midbrain is called the quadrigeminal plate (tectum) and consists of four rounded eminences: the superior colliculi (larger, involved in visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (smaller, involved in auditory reflexes). Above the superior colliculi lies the pineal gland. Below the inferior colliculi lies the superior medullary velum. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) uniquely emerges dorsally just below the inferior colliculus.

explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle is formed by thin membranous structures (medullary vela) and cerebellar components. It contains apertures that allow CSF to circulate between the ventricle and subarachnoid space.
keyConcept: Roof = superior/inferior medullary vela, choroid plexus, foramen of Magendie.
modelAnswer: The roof of the fourth ventricle is divided into superior and inferior parts. The superior roof is formed by the superior medullary velum (white matter between superior cerebellar peduncles) and the lingula of the cerebellum. The inferior roof is formed by the inferior medullary velum, tela choroidea, choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle, and the cerebellar nodule. The roof contains the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and paired lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) for CSF outflow.

explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle (rhomboid fossa) is formed by the dorsal surfaces of the pons and medulla. It contains numerous surface landmarks that overlie important cranial nerve nuclei.
keyConcept: Floor = rhomboid fossa; features median sulcus, foveae, colliculus, striae, trigones.
modelAnswer: The floor of the fourth ventricle is called the rhomboid fossa, formed by the dorsal pons (superior half) and dorsal medulla (inferior half). It is bounded laterally by superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles. Key features include the median sulcus, medial eminence, facial colliculus, superior and inferior foveae, sulcus limitans, hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, vestibular trigone, area postrema, and striae medullares crossing the pontomedullary junction.

explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle are formed predominantly by cerebellar peduncles and related structures, providing passage for CSF through the lateral recesses.
keyConcept: Lateral boundaries = inferior cerebellar peduncle, superior cerebellar peduncle, flocculus, lateral recess.
modelAnswer: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle are formed by the inferior cerebellar peduncles (restiform bodies) inferiorly and the superior cerebellar peduncles (brachia conjunctiva) superiorly. Additional lateral structures include the cuneate tubercle, flocculus, and the lateral recess. The choroid plexus may protrude through the lateral aperture (foramen of Luschka) into the subarachnoid space at the cerebellopontine angle.

explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle contains multiple visible surface structures that correspond to underlying nuclei. These are important clinical landmarks for identifying brainstem lesions.
keyConcept: Rhomboid fossa structures: median sulcus, medial eminence, facial colliculus, foveae, trigones, striae medullares.
modelAnswer: Structures visible in the floor (rhomboid fossa) of the fourth ventricle include: the median sulcus running longitudinally; medial eminence on each side; facial colliculus (a swelling overlying the abducens nucleus); superior fovea and inferior fovea; hypoglossal trigone (most medial structure); vagal trigone; vestibular trigone (between limbs of inferior fovea); area postrema; sulcus limitans; locus coeruleus; auditory tubercle; and striae medullares crossing transversely at the pontomedullary junction.

explanation: The brainstem contains four main ascending sensory lemnisci, each carrying specific modalities from peripheral receptors to thalamic relay nuclei. Understanding their origins, decussations, and terminations is essential for localizing sensory pathway lesions.
keyConcept: Four lemnisci: medial (DCML), lateral (auditory), trigeminal (facial sensation), spinal (pain/temperature).
modelAnswer: There are four main lemnisci: (1) Medial lemniscus arises from gracile and cuneate nuclei after sensory decussation, ascends through medulla, pons and midbrain to terminate in the VPL thalamus, carrying fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception. (2) Lateral lemniscus carries auditory information from cochlear nuclei through superior olivary complex and trapezoid body to the inferior colliculus. (3) Trigeminal lemniscus conveys facial pain, temperature and touch to the VPM thalamus. (4) Spinal lemniscus is formed by spinothalamic fibers carrying pain and temperature from the contralateral body to the VPL thalamus.

explanation: The medulla oblongata contains numerous internal structures including decussations, sensory and motor nuclei, reticular formation, and ascending tracts. These structures are organized topographically and are clinically significant.
keyConcept: Medulla internal features: pyramidal decussation, sensory decussation, olives, cranial nerve nuclei, lemnisci.
modelAnswer: Internal features of the medulla include: the pyramidal decussation (corticospinal fibers crossing caudally), sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei crossing to form medial lemniscus), inferior olivary nucleus and its accessory olives, gracile and cuneate nuclei, nucleus solitarius, hypoglossal nucleus, dorsal vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, vestibular and cochlear nuclei, inferior cerebellar peduncle, reticular formation, and ascending lemnisci (medial, spinal, trigeminal).

explanation: The pyramidal decussation is the crossing point of most corticospinal fibers in the caudal medulla. This decussation explains why motor cortex lesions cause contralateral weakness and why spinal cord lesions cause ipsilateral motor deficits below the lesion.
keyConcept: 85% of corticospinal fibers cross in pyramidal decussation; 15% remain uncrossed as anterior corticospinal tract.
modelAnswer: The pyramidal decussation is located at the caudal end of the medulla oblongata. Approximately 85% of corticospinal tract fibers cross from one side to the other to form the lateral corticospinal tract, which descends in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord. The remaining 15% remain ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract. This decussation explains why lesions above the decussation (e.g., internal capsule stroke) cause contralateral hemiplegia, while spinal cord lesions cause ipsilateral motor deficits.

explanation: The sensory decussation is where second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway cross the midline. This crossing occurs in the caudal medulla and is essential for conveying conscious proprioception and fine touch to the contralateral thalamus and sensory cortex.
keyConcept: 2nd order neurons from gracile/cuneate nuclei cross as internal arcuate fibers to form medial lemniscus.
modelAnswer: The sensory decussation is located in the caudal medulla, where internal arcuate fibers arising from second-order neurons in the gracile and cuneate nuclei sweep ventromedially and cross the midline. After decussating, these fibers ascend contralaterally as the medial lemniscus to terminate in the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus. This pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception from the contralateral side of the body.

explanation: The medulla contains numerous cranial nerve nuclei for CN VIII through CN XII, as well as non-cranial nuclei such as the gracile and cuneate nuclei and inferior olivary nuclei. These nuclei are organized into functional columns and are targets of vascular lesions.
keyConcept: Medullary nuclei include CN VIII-XII nuclei, gracile/cuneate nuclei, inferior olive, and reticular nuclei.
modelAnswer: Nuclei in the medulla oblongata include: cranial nerve nuclei—hypoglossal nucleus (GSE, CN XII), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE, CN X), nucleus ambiguus (SVE, CN IX/X/XI), inferior salivatory nucleus (GVE, CN IX), nucleus solitarius (SVA/GVA, CN VII/IX/X), spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA, CN V/VII/IX/X), vestibular and cochlear nuclei (SSA, CN VIII); non-cranial nuclei—gracile nucleus, cuneate nucleus, inferior olivary nucleus (with medial and dorsal accessory olives), and reticular nuclei.

explanation: The inferior olivary complex is a large convoluted gray matter structure in the ventrolateral medulla that gives rise to climbing fibers projecting to the cerebellum. It plays a critical role in motor coordination and learning.
keyConcept: Inferior olive gives rise to olivocerebellar climbing fibers that cross to enter cerebellum via ICP.
modelAnswer: The inferior olivary complex is a large, convoluted gray matter structure in the ventrolateral medulla. It consists of the principal inferior olivary nucleus, medial accessory olivary nucleus, and dorsal accessory olivary nucleus. It receives inputs from motor cortex, red nucleus, spinal cord, and sensory nuclei. Its neurons give rise to olivocerebellar fibers that decussate and enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, forming climbing fibers that synapse on Purkinje cells. It is essential for motor coordination and motor learning.

explanation: The basis pontis is the ventral portion of the pons, containing descending corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers, pontine nuclei, and transverse pontine fibers that form the middle cerebellar peduncle. It is distinct from the tegmentum dorsally.
keyConcept: Basis pontis = corticospinal/corticonuclear fibers, pontine nuclei, transverse pontine fibers (middle cerebellar peduncle).
modelAnswer: The basis pontis contains: (1) descending corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers running vertically, (2) corticopontine fibers terminating on pontine nuclei, (3) pontine nuclei (clusters of multipolar neurons receiving cortical input), and (4) transverse pontine fibers arising from pontine nuclei, crossing the midline to form the middle cerebellar peduncle projecting to the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere. The reticular formation is NOT in the basis pontis; it lies in the tegmentum.

explanation: The tegmentum of the pons contains multiple cranial nerve nuclei, ascending sensory tracts, and the reticular formation. It is the dorsal portion of the pons, lying between the basis pontis ventrally and the floor of the fourth ventricle dorsally.
keyConcept: Tegmentum pontis contains trigeminal nuclei, abducens/facial nuclei, ascending lemnisci, MLF, and locus coeruleus.
modelAnswer: The tegmentum of the pons contains: cranial nerve nuclei (trigeminal motor and main sensory nuclei, abducens nucleus, facial nucleus, superior olivary nucleus, cochlear nuclei), ascending sensory tracts (medial lemniscus, spinothalamic tract, spinal lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus, lateral lemniscus), the medial longitudinal fasciculus, reticular formation, and locus coeruleus (a noradrenergic nucleus in the rostral pontine tegmentum). The basis pontis lies ventral to the tegmentum.

explanation: The midbrain is divided into three main regions: crus cerebri, tegmentum, and tectum, with the substantia nigra between crus and tegmentum. Each part contains distinct nuclei and fiber tracts essential for motor, sensory, and visual functions.
keyConcept: Midbrain parts: crus cerebri (descending fibers), substantia nigra, tegmentum (red nucleus, nuclei), tectum (colliculi).
modelAnswer: The midbrain contains three main parts: (1) Crus cerebri (most ventral)—contains corticospinal, corticonuclear, frontopontine, and parietotemporoccipitopontine fibers. (2) Substantia nigra—between crus and tegmentum, with pars compacta (dopaminergic) and pars reticulata (GABAergic). (3) Tegmentum—contains red nucleus, oculomotor and trochlear nuclei, reticular formation, medial lemniscus, spinothalamic tract, and decussation of superior cerebellar peduncle. (4) Tectum (dorsal)—contains superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (auditory reflexes).

explanation: The crus cerebri contains multiple descending fiber tracts organized somatotopically from medial to lateral. Understanding this organization is important for localizing lesions that produce specific motor or coordination deficits.
keyConcept: Crus cerebri: medial 1/5 frontopontine, middle 3/5 corticospinal/corticonuclear, lateral 1/5 parietotemporoccipitopontine.
modelAnswer: The crus cerebri contains descending fiber tracts arranged somatotopically: the medial one-fifth contains frontopontine fibers from the frontal lobe; the middle three-fifths contain corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers (with corticospinal fibers placed laterally within this middle group); and the lateral one-fifth contains parietopontine, temporopontine, and occipitopontine fibers from the respective cortical association areas, all terminating in pontine nuclei.

explanation: The midbrain contains two decussations in its tegmentum: the dorsal tegmental decussation (tectospinal fibers from superior colliculus) and the ventral tegmental decussation (rubrospinal fibers from red nucleus). These decussations coordinate head-eye movements and upper limb flexion respectively.
keyConcept: Tegmental decussations: dorsal (tectospinal, superior colliculus) and ventral (rubrospinal, red nucleus).
modelAnswer: The midbrain contains two tegmental decussations: (1) Dorsal tegmental decussation (Meynert)—located near the superior colliculus, formed by tectospinal tract fibers crossing to control reflexive head-turning to visual stimuli. (2) Ventral tegmental decussation (Forel)—located at the level of the red nucleus, formed by rubrospinal tract fibers crossing before descending in the lateral funiculus to facilitate upper limb flexion.

explanation: The vagus nerve has four main nuclei in the medulla: dorsal vagal nucleus (parasympathetic), nucleus ambiguus (branchial muscles), nucleus solitarius (taste and visceral sensation), and spinal trigeminal nucleus (general sensation). Each serves distinct visceral and somatic functions.
keyConcept: Vagus nuclei: dorsal vagal (GVE), ambiguus (SVE), solitarius (SVA/GVA), spinal trigeminal (GSA).
modelAnswer: The vagus nerve (CN X) has four main nuclei: (1) Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE)—preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to smooth muscle and glands of pharynx, larynx, esophagus, and thoracoabdominal viscera. (2) Nucleus ambiguus (SVE)—supplies pharyngeal constrictors and all intrinsic laryngeal muscles via recurrent laryngeal nerve. (3) Nucleus solitarius—receives taste from epiglottis and general visceral afferent input (baroreceptors, chemoreceptors). (4) Spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA)—receives pain, temperature, and touch from posterior auricular skin, external auditory meatus, and laryngeal/pharyngeal mucosa.

explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve has four main nuclei: inferior salivatory nucleus (parasympathetic to parotid), nucleus ambiguus (stylopharyngeus), nucleus solitarius (taste and carotid baroreception), and spinal trigeminal nucleus (general sensation).
keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nuclei: inferior salivatory (GVE), ambiguus (SVE), solitarius (SVA/GVA), spinal trigeminal (GSA).
modelAnswer: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) has four nuclei: (1) Inferior salivatory nucleus (GVE)—preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to parotid gland via otic ganglion. (2) Nucleus ambiguus (SVE)—innervates stylopharyngeus muscle. (3) Nucleus solitarius—receives taste from posterior one-third of tongue (SVA) and general visceral afferent from carotid sinus baroreceptors and carotid body chemoreceptors (GVA). (4) Spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA)—receives general sensation from posterior tongue, tonsil, and oropharynx.

explanation: The facial nerve has four associated nuclei: facial motor nucleus (muscles of facial expression), superior salivatory nucleus (lacrimal, nasal, submandibular, sublingual glands), nucleus solitarius (taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue), and spinal trigeminal nucleus (general sensation from external ear).
keyConcept: Facial nerve nuclei: motor (SVE), superior salivatory (GVE), solitarius (SVA), spinal trigeminal (GSA).
modelAnswer: The facial nerve (CN VII) is associated with four nuclei: (1) Facial motor nucleus (SVE)—innervates all muscles of facial expression, posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid, and stapedius. (2) Superior salivatory nucleus (GVE)—preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal gland (pterygopalatine ganglion) and submandibular/sublingual glands (submandibular ganglion). (3) Nucleus solitarius (SVA)—receives taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani. (4) Spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA)—receives general sensation from skin behind the ear.

explanation: The trigeminal nerve has four nuclei: motor nucleus (muscles of mastication), principal sensory nucleus (facial touch), spinal trigeminal nucleus (facial pain/temperature), and mesencephalic nucleus (proprioception from mastication). These nuclei span from midbrain to upper cervical spinal cord.
keyConcept: Trigeminal nuclei: motor (SVE), principal sensory (GSA touch), spinal (GSA pain/temperature), mesencephalic (GSA proprioception).
modelAnswer: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) has four nuclei: (1) Motor nucleus (SVE)—innervates muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, pterygoids), tensor tympani, tensor palati, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric. (2) Principal sensory nucleus (GSA light touch)—located in the pons, receives discriminative touch from the face. (3) Spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA pain/temperature)—extends from pons to C2 spinal cord, receives pain and temperature from face, cornea, nasal and oral cavities. (4) Mesencephalic nucleus (GSA proprioception)—contains primary pseudounipolar neurons for proprioception from mastication muscles and periodontal ligaments.

explanation: The oculomotor nerve originates from two nuclei in the midbrain periaqueductal gray: the oculomotor nucleus (somatic motor to extraocular muscles and levator palpebrae) and the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle).
keyConcept: Oculomotor nuclei: main nucleus (GSE to extraocular muscles + levator) and E-W nucleus (GVE to pupil and ciliary muscle).
modelAnswer: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) arises from two nuclei: (1) Oculomotor nucleus (GSE)—in the periaqueductal gray at the level of the superior colliculus, innervates superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris. (2) Edinger-Westphal nucleus (GVE)—located dorsal to the main nucleus, sends preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in the ciliary ganglion. Postganglionic fibers innervate the sphincter pupillae (pupillary constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation).

explanation: The general somatic efferent (GSE) column contains four nuclei that innervate skeletal muscles derived from somites (myotomes). These include the extraocular muscle nuclei and the hypoglossal nucleus.
keyConcept: GSE column: CN III, IV, VI (extraocular muscles) and CN XII (tongue muscles).
modelAnswer: The GSE column contains four nuclei: (1) Oculomotor nucleus (CN III)—supplies superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris. (2) Trochlear nucleus (CN IV)—supplies superior oblique. (3) Abducens nucleus (CN VI)—supplies lateral rectus. (4) Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII)—supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (which is supplied by CN X).

explanation: The special visceral efferent (SVE) or branchiomotor column innervates muscles derived from pharyngeal arches. It includes the trigeminal motor nucleus (first arch), facial motor nucleus (second arch), and nucleus ambiguus (third to sixth arches).
keyConcept: SVE column: trigeminal motor (1st arch), facial motor (2nd arch), nucleus ambiguus (3rd-6th arches).
modelAnswer: The SVE column contains three nuclei: (1) Trigeminal motor nucleus (CN V)—supplies first pharyngeal arch muscles: temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids, tensor tympani, tensor palati, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric. (2) Facial motor nucleus (CN VII)—supplies second pharyngeal arch muscles: all muscles of facial expression, posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid, and stapedius. (3) Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI)—supplies third to sixth pharyngeal arch muscles: stylopharyngeus (IX), pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles (X), and trapezius/sternocleidomastoid (spinal accessory, XI).

explanation: The general visceral efferent (GVE) column contains parasympathetic preganglionic nuclei. These include the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III), superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII), inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX), and dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (CN X).
keyConcept: GVE column = parasympathetic nuclei: E-W (CN III), superior salivatory (CN VII), inferior salivatory (CN IX), dorsal vagal (CN X).
modelAnswer: The GVE column contains four parasympathetic nuclei: (1) Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III)—innervates sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle via ciliary ganglion. (2) Superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII)—innervates lacrimal gland (pterygopalatine ganglion), submandibular and sublingual glands (submandibular ganglion). (3) Inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX)—innervates parotid gland (otic ganglion). (4) Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (CN X)—innervates smooth muscle and glands of thoracoabdominal viscera (heart, lungs, esophagus, stomach, intestines).

explanation: The general somatic afferent (GSA) column for cranial nerves is represented primarily by the trigeminal sensory nuclei: principal sensory nucleus (light touch), spinal trigeminal nucleus (pain/temperature), and mesencephalic nucleus (proprioception). The vestibulocochlear nuclei are special somatic afferent (SSA), not GSA.
keyConcept: GSA column: principal sensory nucleus (touch), spinal trigeminal nucleus (pain/temperature), mesencephalic nucleus (proprioception).
modelAnswer: The GSA column includes: (1) Spinal trigeminal nucleus—receives pain and temperature from the face, nasal cavity, oral cavity, and cornea via CN V, VII, IX, X. (2) Principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal nerve—receives discriminative touch and proprioception from the face. (3) Mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve—receives unconscious proprioception from muscles of mastication, temporomandibular joint, and periodontal ligaments. Note that vestibular and cochlear nuclei are SSA (special somatic afferent), not GSA.

explanation: The medulla oblongata receives a rich blood supply from the vertebral arteries, anterior spinal artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), and posterior spinal arteries. Each vessel supplies specific territories, and their occlusion produces distinct clinical syndromes.
keyConcept: Medulla supply = vertebral + anterior spinal + PICA + posterior spinal arteries.
modelAnswer: The medulla is supplied by: (1) Vertebral arteries—give direct medullary branches and the anterior spinal artery. (2) Anterior spinal artery—supplies medial medulla (pyramid, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus). (3) Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)—supplies lateral medulla (inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular nuclei, spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus). Occlusion causes Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome. (4) Posterior spinal arteries—supply dorsal medulla (gracile and cuneate nuclei and tubercles).
